title: The Open-Plan Office
context: 開放式辦公室的理想與現實
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

paragraphs.text: The open-plan office, in which employees sit together in one large room rather than in separate enclosed ones, is often thought of as a recent fashion. In fact it is more than a century old. The clerks of the early 1900s sat at long rows of identical desks under the eye of a supervisor, an arrangement borrowed directly from the factory floor and intended, like the factory, to make work visible and measurable. Private rooms were for managers. Space, in other words, expressed rank.

The first serious attempt to rethink this layout came from Germany in the late 1950s. Two brothers who ran a consultancy near Hamburg proposed what they called the 'office landscape'. Desks were arranged in loose, irregular groups according to who needed to talk to whom, with plants and movable screens in place of walls, and managers sat among their staff. The aim was not to save money but to improve the flow of information, and the scheme required generous amounts of room. It was widely admired, and widely misunderstood.

A second idealist was the American designer Robert Propst, who spent years observing how office employees actually worked. He concluded that they needed both privacy and freedom of movement, and in 1968 he introduced a system of low partitions set at wide angles, which each worker could rearrange and which provided surfaces at different heights for standing or sitting. Companies saw a different possibility. By straightening the angles and shrinking the space, they found they could pack more people into a floor than ever before, and the partitions were cheaper than walls and could be treated more favourably for tax purposes. The result was the cubicle. Propst, who lived until 2000, came to regard what had been done with his invention with dismay.

By the end of the century the cubicle had become a symbol of dull corporate life, and a new generation of technology firms made a point of abolishing it. Their offices had no partitions at all: long shared tables, few fixed places, and a great deal of talk about spontaneity. Employees who bumped into one another, the argument ran, would exchange ideas, and ideas were what such companies sold. Older businesses hurried to imitate them. The fact that an open floor accommodates more people per square metre, and therefore costs less in rent, was mentioned less often, though it was seldom far from the minds of those who approved the plans.

Whether open offices actually produce the promised collaboration was, remarkably, not tested with any rigour until 2018. In that year two researchers at Harvard Business School, Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban, studied two large companies that were removing the partitions from their offices. Rather than asking employees for their impressions, they had them wear electronic badges that recorded when they spoke to one another. After the change, face-to-face conversation fell by about seventy per cent, while the number of emails and instant messages rose. Exposed to view on all sides, people appeared to withdraw: they put on headphones, avoided disturbing their neighbours, and communicated through their screens.

This finding fits a larger body of survey evidence. Workers in open offices consistently report more difficulty in concentrating than those in enclosed ones, and the complaint they make most often concerns noise – in particular, other people's conversations, which the brain finds far harder to ignore than a steady mechanical hum. They also report less satisfaction with their privacy. Several studies have found that employees in open offices take more days of sick leave, though whether this is because infections spread more easily or because the environment is more stressful has not been established.

None of this means that the walls should simply go back up. A private room for every employee is beyond the means of most organisations, and people who work in teams do need to be within reach of one another. The more thoughtful recent designs offer variety instead: quiet rooms for concentrated work, small booths for telephone calls, and open areas for discussion, with employees moving between them as the task requires. Such arrangements work, however, only when there are enough quiet spaces to go round, and that returns us to the point on which the idealists of the 1950s and 1960s were defeated. Good offices need space, and space is exactly what those who pay for offices are most reluctant to provide.

items.stem: What point does the writer make about offices in the early 1900s?

options.A: They were designed to encourage discussion among clerks.
options.B: Their layout reflected the status of the people who worked in them.
options.C: They were more comfortable than the factories of the time.
options.D: They were the first workplaces to employ supervisors.

items.stem: The main purpose of the 'office landscape' was to

options.A: reduce the amount companies spent on office space.
options.B: allow managers to watch their staff more closely.
options.C: help information pass more easily between people.
options.D: make offices more attractive by adding plants.

items.stem: What does the writer say about Robert Propst's system?

options.A: It was developed from the German 'office landscape'.
options.B: It was used by companies in a way he had not intended.
options.C: It proved too expensive for most companies to buy.
options.D: It was unpopular because workers could not adjust it.

items.stem: According to the writer, technology firms claimed that offices without partitions would

options.A: cut the amount they paid in rent.
options.B: encourage employees to work for longer.
options.C: help older businesses to compete with them.
options.D: lead to chance meetings in which ideas were shared.

items.stem: What was distinctive about the method used in the 2018 study?

options.A: It recorded what people did instead of asking for their opinions.
options.B: It compared companies in several different countries.
options.C: It depended on employees' own reports of their behaviour.
options.D: It followed the same employees for a number of years.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
groups.limit:
Write
YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

items.text: Those who promoted partition-free offices openly emphasised the money that would be saved.
The findings of the 2018 study contradicted the claims that had been made for open offices.
Mechanical noise is more distracting than the sound of other people talking.
Employees in open offices are paid less than those who have private rooms.
Offices that provide a variety of spaces succeed only if they contain a sufficient number of quiet areas.

groups.instruction: Complete the summary using the list of words, A–H, below.
groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–H, next to Questions 37–40.
groups.title: Two idealists

rows.text: In the German 'office landscape', desks were grouped according to patterns of {37}, and the scheme needed a large amount of {38}. Robert Propst's system was intended to give workers privacy and freedom of {39}. Companies, however, used it to fit more employees onto each floor, and the partitions also brought advantages in terms of {40}.

questions.explain:
答案是 B。職員坐在一排排相同的桌子前，獨立的房間是給主管的，作者總結 Space, in other words, expressed rank。
同義轉換：expressed rank ＝ reflected the status。
陷阱：A 相反，這種安排是為了讓工作 visible and measurable（看得見、可衡量），不是鼓勵討論。
questions.quote: Space, in other words, expressed rank.

questions.explain:
答案是 C。原文 The aim was not to save money but to improve the flow of information。
陷阱：A 被 not to save money 直接否定；D 的植物只是用來取代牆壁的手段，不是目的。not A but B 的句型，答案在 but 之後。
questions.quote: The aim was not to save money but to improve the flow of information

questions.explain:
答案是 B。Propst 想給員工隱私和活動的自由，Companies saw a different possibility：把角度拉直、空間縮小，塞進更多人，結果變成小隔間。他後來對此感到 dismay。
陷阱：D 相反，原本的設計是 each worker could rearrange；C 也相反，隔板比牆便宜。
questions.quote: came to regard what had been done with his invention with dismay

questions.explain:
答案是 D。科技公司的說法是：Employees who bumped into one another... would exchange ideas。
同義轉換：bumped into one another ＝ chance meetings；exchange ideas ＝ ideas were shared。
陷阱：A 的租金是真實的好處，但文章說這一點 was mentioned less often。題目問的是公司「聲稱」的理由。
questions.quote: Employees who bumped into one another, the argument ran, would exchange ideas

questions.explain:
答案是 A。研究者 Rather than asking employees for their impressions，讓員工配戴電子識別證，記錄他們何時交談。
陷阱：C 正是研究者刻意「不採用」的方法。Rather than 之後是被捨棄的做法。
questions.quote: Rather than asking employees for their impressions, they had them wear electronic badges that recorded when they spoke to one another.

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。開放樓層能省租金這件事 was mentioned less often，雖然批准計畫的人心裡一直記著。
解題關鍵：mentioned less often 與題目的 openly emphasised 相反。
questions.quote: was mentioned less often, though it was seldom far from the minds of those who approved the plans

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。開放式辦公室號稱能促進合作，但研究發現拆掉隔板後 face-to-face conversation fell by about seventy per cent。
解題關鍵：承諾的是更多交流，實測卻是面對面交談大減，結果與宣稱相反。
questions.quote: After the change, face-to-face conversation fell by about seventy per cent

questions.explain:
答案是 NO。別人的談話是 far harder to ignore than a steady mechanical hum，也就是人聲比機械聲更干擾。
解題關鍵：題目把比較的方向反過來了。
questions.quote: other people's conversations, which the brain finds far harder to ignore than a steady mechanical hum

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章比較了兩種辦公室的專注程度、隱私滿意度和病假天數，但完全沒有提到薪水。
陷阱：第一段說獨立房間是給主管的，容易聯想到薪水差異，但那是一百年前的情況，而且文章也沒談薪水。
questions.quote: They also report less satisfaction with their privacy.

questions.explain:
答案是 YES。原文 Such arrangements work, however, only when there are enough quiet spaces to go round。
同義轉換：work only when ＝ succeed only if；enough quiet spaces to go round ＝ a sufficient number of quiet areas。
questions.quote: Such arrangements work, however, only when there are enough quiet spaces to go round

questions.explain:
答案是 A（communication）。桌子的分組是 according to who needed to talk to whom，也就是依照溝通的需要。
陷阱：B（rank）是二十世紀初舊式辦公室的原則；office landscape 裡主管就坐在員工之間，不按階級安排。
questions.quote: Desks were arranged in loose, irregular groups according to who needed to talk to whom

questions.explain:
答案是 C（space）。原文 the scheme required generous amounts of room。
同義轉換：generous amounts of room ＝ a large amount of space。
questions.quote: the scheme required generous amounts of room

questions.explain:
答案是 E（movement）。Propst 認為員工需要 both privacy and freedom of movement。
陷阱：F（speech）是刻意的干擾項，freedom of speech 是常見的搭配，但文章寫的是 freedom of movement。
questions.quote: He concluded that they needed both privacy and freedom of movement

questions.explain:
答案是 G（tax）。隔板 were cheaper than walls and could be treated more favourably for tax purposes。
解題關鍵：treated more favourably for tax purposes ＝ advantages in terms of tax。
questions.quote: the partitions were cheaper than walls and could be treated more favourably for tax purposes
